blurb: A rounded clump of deeply cut dark green leaves throwing silky-haired wiry stems that carry cupped flowers in white through pink to a surprising brick-red. Note the name: this is not the guide's Grecian windflower, and every fresh part of it is poisonous.
water: Low to moderate; occasional deep soak in summer heat
spread: Clumping from a woody crown; spreads only by seed
seasons: White to pink-red cups May–August on wiry stems; deeply cut dark foliage; dies back in winter
wildlife: Native bees and butterflies work the flowers

care.hardiness: CSU lists this as a Colorado native plantable to about 10,000 ft, so cold is not the constraint at Boulder's zone 5b–6a.[1]
care.planting: Plant in spring after the mid-May last frost, or in early fall, into ground prepared to suit it (see Soil). Set out young container plants — most of these natives resent having an established root system disturbed — and water them in well, then taper off.[1][2]
care.sun: Full sun to part shade, which is CSU's exposure rating for it.[1]
care.soil: CSU specifies organic soils for this one, and the Wildflower Center adds gravelly, calcareous ground with medium moisture. So: work compost into it, keep it draining, and don't treat it as a bone-dry xeric plant.[1][3]
care.water: Low to moderate. CSU rates its moisture requirement low to moderate, and on the semi-arid Front Range that is the number that matters most — the commonest way to kill a xeric native here is kindness with the hose.[1][2]
care.spacing: Space to suit its mature spread of 12–18 in wide. Deeply cut dark green leaves forming a rounded clump, with flowers borne on wiry stems — CSU specifies organic soils.[1]
care.propagation: By seed, which is how nearly all of these natives are raised and how they persist in a planting. Autumn sowing outdoors lets winter provide the chilling most of them want.[1]
care.bloom: Flowers from spring into midsummer; CSU records the colour as white, pink, red and the height as 12–24 in tall.[1][3]
care.maintenance: The Wildflower Center notes the species is highly variable and advises sourcing local material matched to your site. It also takes more shade than most of this list — sun, part shade or shade.[1][3]
care.troubles: Few pests or diseases when it is sited right. Crown and root rot in soil that stays wet is the usual cause of failure for a Colorado native in a Front Range garden, and it is a siting problem rather than bad luck.[1][2]

edible.summary: Poisonous. The Wildflower Center states that all fresh parts of the plant are poisonous.[1][3]
edible.caution: Do not eat any part of this plant. The Wildflower Center is explicit that **all fresh plant parts are poisonous**, with inflammation and blistering on contact with the fresh sap, and irritation of the mouth, vomiting and diarrhoea if it is swallowed in quantity. That is the buttercup family (Ranunculaceae) acting as it usually does. Wear gloves when cutting it back, keep the sap away from eyes, and site it away from where children or pets graze. Drying reduces the irritant, but that is not a reason to treat it as food.[1][3]
